# Prose and Markdown

Full rules, evidence and examples: `common/writing/prose.md`.

- DOC-01 prefer: Describe a thing in one clause; in a list of fragments use no trailing period, in a list of full sentences use periods, and do not mix inside one list.
- DOC-02 must: Write headings in Title Case without trailing punctuation, one H1, no skipped levels; number only the steps of an ordered how-to.
  Good: `## Continuous Integration and Automations`
- DOC-03 must: Link on first mention as `[Name](url)`, wrap bare URLs in `<...>`, link internal files with a backticked relative path (a link whose label is a backticked path is fine), and use anchors for in-page jumps.
  Good: link `[Renovate](url)` once, wrap `<https://example.org/docs>`, and point to ``docs/setup.md`` in backticks.
  Bad: a bare `https://example.org/docs` mid-sentence, or a second link to the same name.
- DOC-04 must: Give every fenced block a language: `bash` for commands, `yaml`, `go`, `python`, `txt` for output, `text` for trees.
  Good: a fence opened with `bash` for `mise install` and `txt` for its output.
  Bad: a fence with no language, or `shell`.
- DOC-05 must: Use `-` for bullets, two-space nested indent and `- [x]` / `- [ ]` for status inventories.
  Good: `- [x] vault` with a nested `- [ ] backup` indented two spaces.
  Bad: `* vault` with four-space nesting.
- DOC-06 must: Write Markdown prose as one paragraph per line, without hard wraps; code comments follow the formatter's line length.
  Good: one paragraph on one line, however long it runs.
  Bad: the same paragraph broken at 80 columns.
- DOC-08 must: In alerts, end no line with trailing spaces; put each line on its own `>` line.
  Good: `> [!WARNING]` then `> Deleting the volume loses all data.` then `> Back it up first.`
  Bad: a line ending in two trailing spaces for a hard break.
- DOC-09 lean: Bold only the decision-bearing phrase of a sentence, and use it rarely.
- DOC-10 prefer: Put a comma before "and" only where it prevents ambiguity or helps clarity; otherwise omit it.
- DOC-11 prefer: Use American spelling.
- DOC-13 prefer: Give a surprising behavior's cause in the same sentence after a colon or semicolon, not in a separate paragraph.
- DOC-14 prefer: Document a breaking release with a version-mapping row, a "Migration from A to B" section and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` commit footer.
- DOC-15 prefer: Write agent instructions as short imperative fragments with numeric limits; put one rule per bullet and add a rationale only when the exception matters.
- DOC-16 lean: State agent boundaries as a closed list: what the agent may do, what needs a one-off approval, what stays with the owner.
- DOC-17 prefer: Use GitHub alert blockquotes (`[!IMPORTANT]`, `[!WARNING]`, `[!NOTE]`, `[!CAUTION]`) only for caveats that can break things, one per caveat: the first line gives the consequence, the next the remedy.
- DOC-18 must: Put everything the reader is meant to copy (commands to run, prompts, instructions to paste into a config, snippets) in a fenced code block with a language tag (`bash`, `text`, `yaml`), written so it works as pasted; a command or file only named in running text stays inline code, as in README-05's Development opener.
  Good: "Add this to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`:" followed by a fenced `text` block with the instruction.
  Bad: an instruction to paste written inside a sentence in quotes.

Avoid (AI-Era Artifacts):

- Em dashes, emoji, banners (PRIN-11 to PRIN-13).
- Hard-wrapped paragraphs at 80 to 120 columns.
- Sentence-case headings such as "Repository layout".
- Marketing phrases and feature walls ("integrates seamlessly").
- A new README section per change (PRIN-07).
- Typos the owner leaves ("needs to exists", "udpate readme") are not style; fix them when touching the text.
